original_question: The paper restricts the parameters c0 and d0 to be real numbers throughout the osp(1|2) analysis. If one allows c0 and/or d0 to take imaginary values instead, does the obstruction to completing the osp(1|2) triangle-sum-rule derivation change, and can such an extension lead to a valid final solution?
target_in_paper: The closest paper-faithful target is the paper’s open problem of completing the final identification step in the real-parameter osp(1|2) intrinsic-operator calculation—equivalently, finding general formulas for the unknown polynomials P^π(λ,κ) (and conjecturally related Q^π(λ,κ)) or for their binomial expansion coefficients x over (c0+d0^2)^(Ω-m)(d0^2)^m—so as to obtain a genuine osp(1|2) super-triangle sum rule with 6-j^S symbols and the supertriangle Δ^S.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies two real features of the paper: (i) the osp(1|2) analysis is carried out with real parameters c0 and d0, and (ii) the derivation runs into an obstruction at the final identification stage, so the hoped-for osp(1|2) triangle/super-triangle sum rule is not completed. It also correctly treats the issue as one about whether the derivation can be finished to give a valid final formula.
missing_details: The paper does not formulate the open problem as an extension to imaginary or complex values of c0 or d0; it keeps c0,d0 in R and asks whether the derivation can be completed within that real setup.
The paper’s actual target is a veritable osp(1|2) super-triangle sum rule involving 6-j^S symbols and the supertriangle Δ^S, not merely a statement about parameter domains.
The question should specify the intrinsic-operator framework: iterated osp(1|2) tensor operators S^κ(c0,d0) built from a basic rank-1/2 operator.
The obstruction is tied to the final identification over the two combinations c0+d0^2 and d0^2, more precisely over binomials of the form (c0+d0^2)^(Ω-m)(d0^2)^m.
The unknown objects that actually block the proof are the polynomials P^π(λ,κ) and their expansion coefficients x; without naming these, the obstruction is not paper-faithful.
Conjecture 1 should be mentioned: the coefficients x are conjectured to be integers.
If the lowest-rank closure relations are included, the paper also introduces Q^π(λ,κ) and conjectures Q^π(λ,κ)=P^π(λ,κ-λ+π); your draft omits this nearby paper-specific reformulation.
The admissible labels/ranks should be stated: the paper works with integral and half-integral rank labels (e.g. the appendix distinguishes integral p from half-integral π).
The question should quantify over all admissible ranks/spins for which the closure relations and 6-j^S symbols are defined, rather than asking only whether some altered scalar choice might help.
Your draft does not indicate that the paper explicitly concludes that the main obstacle is the lack of a general formula for x, leading to an analytical dead end in the identification process.

No paper-critical nilpotency, homogeneity, or degree restriction is part of this problem; the essential missing structure is instead the tensor-operator setup, the real parameter domain, the binomial basis, and the quantification over admissible ranks.
refined_question: Within Bréhamet’s intrinsic-operator construction of iterated osp(1|2) tensor operators S^κ(c0,d0) from a basic rank-1/2 operator, with c0,d0 in R and closure relations expressed using the supertriangle Δ^S, can one determine, for every admissible integral or half-integral rank configuration (λ,κ,π), a general closed formula for the polynomials P^π(λ,κ)—equivalently for their binomial expansion coefficients x (conjecturally integers) in the basis (c0+d0^2)^(Ω-m)(d0^2)^m, and hence also for Q^π(λ,κ) if Conjecture 2 holds—so that the final identification step in the triple-tensor-product calculation closes and yields a genuine osp(1|2) super-triangle sum rule in terms of 6-j^S symbols and Δ^S?
justification: The paper’s abstract and conclusion repeatedly frame the unresolved issue not as a question about extending c0,d0 beyond the reals, but as the failure of the final identification process in the osp(1|2) calculation because the relevant polynomials P and their coefficients x are not known in general. The introduction then pinpoints the precise nearby structure: Section 6 fixes two independent real variables c0 and d0 for S^κ(c0,d0); Section 8 introduces the polynomials P^π(λ,κ) and Conjecture 1 on integrality of x; Sections 9–10 introduce Q^π and Conjecture 2; Section 12 reaches the penultimate triple-product stage; and the end of Section 13 plus the conclusion say that this sets the open problem and that the final identification over c0+d0^2 and d0^2 runs into an analytical dead end. Appendix A.4 further shows that special generator conditions depend on c0+d0^2, but the paper does not turn this into a complex-parameter extension question. So the nearest official formulation to your draft is the open problem of determining P/Q or x well enough to complete the real-parameter derivation of the osp(1|2) super-triangle sum rule.
